difficultyRationale: Standard AP-style argumentation FRQ. Students craft a claim, select evidence from three short sources, and explain it with two different psychological concepts (sleep deprivation effects on attention, research design strengths and limits such as random assignment, confounds, and significance). Needs multi-step reasoning and discrimination of evidence quality, but all content is in scope and the sources are brief and clear. No computation. Difficulty comes from the skill, not from unfair sources.

payload.title: Later school start times
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A laboratory experiment on sleep and attention
Researchers randomly assigned 60 high school students to spend either six hours or eight hours in bed for three nights. On the fourth morning, all students completed a 30-minute attention task in which they pressed a key when a target appeared among distractors. The mean accuracy was 71 percent for the six-hour group (30 students) and 85 percent for the eight-hour group (30 students). The difference was statistically significant.

Source 2: A survey of students in two districts
Researchers surveyed 1,200 high school students about their sleep. Students in the district whose school day began at 7:15 a.m. (600 students) reported an average of 6.4 hours of sleep on school nights. Students in the district whose school day began at 8:45 a.m. (600 students) reported an average of 7.6 hours. The researchers noted that the districts were not assigned to start times and may differ in other ways, such as family income.

Source 3: A comparison of grades before and after a schedule change
Researchers followed one school that moved its start time from 7:15 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. The mean grade-point average of the students was 2.90 in the year before the change and 3.02 in the year after. The researchers reported that the difference was not statistically significant (p = .18) and noted that the school also changed some course offerings in the same year.

stimulus.description: Summary of the key results in the three sources

rows: Mean attention accuracy: 71% (six hours in bed) vs 85% (eight hours in bed); statistically significant
Average sleep on school nights: 6.4 hours (7:15 start) vs 7.6 hours (8:45 start)
Mean GPA 2.90 before vs 3.02 after; not statistically significant; course offerings also changed

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim, based in psychological science, that responds to the question: Should a school district move the start of the school day later for high school students?
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. A district should start the high school day later, because the evidence shows that more sleep improves students' attention and later starts are linked to more sleep.

rubric_rows.criterion: Proposes a specific and defensible claim that responds to the question
required_elements: Proposes a claim that is relevant to the question and takes a position or states a specific effect or recommendation (not a restatement of the question or an oversimplified conclusion)
alt_solutions: High schools should move to a later start time, because students who sleep more perform better on attention tasks.
A district should consider a later start for high school students, because later starts are linked to more sleep even though the evidence that grades improve is weak.
common_errors: describes the question without making a claim
proposes a claim that is unrelated to the question
states that the issue is difficult or complicated without taking a position
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Support your claim with one specific and relevant piece of evidence from one of the three sources. Cite the source (for example, 'Source 1').
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. Source 1: students who spent eight hours in bed had a mean accuracy of 85 percent on the attention task, compared with 71 percent for students who spent six hours in bed.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses one specific, accurate, and correctly cited piece of evidence from one source
required_elements: Cites one source (Source 1, 2, or 3) and gives specific and relevant evidence from it that supports the student's claim, such as a number or finding
alt_solutions: Source 2: 7.6 hours versus 6.4 hours of sleep
Source 3: mean GPA rose from 2.90 to 3.02
common_errors: gives a vague statement such as 'the sources say sleep matters'
gives evidence that is not relevant to the claim
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence you used in part B supports your claim, using a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding that you learned in AP Psychology.
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. Sleep loss impairs attention: when students sleep less, they have more difficulty focusing on a task (selective attention) and filtering out distractors, which explains why the six-hour group was less accurate.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the relationship between the evidence and the claim
required_elements: explains how the evidence supports the claim: students with more sleep performed better, which supports a later start that allows more sleep
links the evidence to the claim by showing how the amount of sleep changes performance
alt_solutions: students who slept more performed better, which supports giving students more time to sleep
the difference in attention shows that sleep amount changes performance, so the claim is supported
common_errors: identifies the evidence without explaining how it relates to the claim
gives an opinion that does not refer to the sources
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding
required_elements: Applies a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding from the course, such as selective attention, the effects of sleep deprivation on attention, encoding, or memory consolidation during sleep, to explain how the evidence supports the claim
alt_solutions: selective attention was reduced by sleep loss
sleep loss impairs attention, so the sleep-deprived group made more errors
memory consolidation during sleep: less sleep means less consolidation
common_errors: uses a concept that is only a term from the source such as 'sleep' or 'mean' or 'survey'
uses the same concept as in the earlier explanation part
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Support your claim with an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source than the source you used in part B. Cite the source.
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. Source 2: students in the district with an 8:45 a.m. start reported an average of 7.6 hours of sleep on school nights, compared with 6.4 hours in the district with a 7:15 a.m. start.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses one specific, accurate, and correctly cited piece of evidence from a different source than part B
required_elements: Cites a different source from the one used in part B and gives specific and relevant evidence from it that supports the claim
alt_solutions: Source 2: 7.6 hours versus 6.4 hours of sleep
Source 3: mean GPA rose from 2.90 to 3.02
Source 1: 85% versus 71% (if Source 2 or 3 was used in part B)
common_errors: uses the same source as part B
gives evidence that is not relevant to the claim
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence you used in part D supports your claim, using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding than the one you used in part C.
parts.model_answer: ALTON reference answer for self-review — not official AP scoring. Circadian rhythm: during adolescence the body's internal clock shifts so that teenagers tend to feel sleepy later at night and wake later in the morning, so an early start conflicts with their rhythm and cuts their sleep, which a later start would reduce.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the relationship between the evidence and the claim
required_elements: explains how the evidence supports the claim: later starts matched with more hours of sleep, which supports changing the schedule
links the evidence to the claim by showing that sleep amount is tied to start time
alt_solutions: more sleep went with later starts, which supports changing the schedule
the sleep difference between the districts links start time to the amount of sleep, so the claim is supported
common_errors: identifies the evidence without explaining how it relates to the claim
gives an opinion that does not refer to the sources
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding
required_elements: Applies a different psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding from the course than the one used in part C, such as circadian rhythm, melatonin, sleep stages, or the effects of sleep deprivation on mood
alt_solutions: melatonin is released later at night in teenagers
the body's internal clock makes early wake times hard for teenagers
common_errors: uses a concept that is only a term from the source such as 'sleep' or 'mean' or 'survey'
uses the same concept as in the earlier explanation part
rubric_rows.grading_note: Award the point when the response conveys the required meaning, whatever the wording; do not require any specific phrase.

review.summary: Original EBQ on later school start times with three consistent fictional sources and a 7-point structure (1/1/2/1/2). The content is in scope (sleep deprivation and attention, circadian rhythm). The rubric is meaning-based and the model answers use numbers readable from the sources. The independent solver reached the same answers. One minor weakness: the Part D alternatives accept the nonsignificant, confounded Source 3 result as supporting evidence without qualification, which is loose for a 4.B skill, but it is not a wrong key.

scope_skill.notes: Content is within 1.5 and 2.1. Parts B and D target 4.B, and parts C and E are tagged 1.A by design.

key_scoring.notes: Rubric rows are analytic and consistent. Each source supports at least two defensible claims and two different course concepts. A minor looseness is that Source 3 (p = .18, confounded) is accepted as support in D alt_solutions.

stimulus_expression.notes: The table and source text are complete and consistent, and every number in the model answers is readable from the sources.

distractor_explanation.notes: This is an FRQ, so there are no options. Common errors are listed for each rubric row.

exam_suitability.notes: The 7-point EBQ load and structure match the official task format, with no calculator needed.
